title: Why Anaesthesia Still Lacks an Explanation
paragraphs: Every year tens of millions of people receive a drug, lose consciousness within seconds, lie still while their bodies are opened, and wake with nothing to report.
The procedure is also remarkably safe, with deaths attributable to the anaesthetic counted in cases per hundreds of thousands.
What is strange about this success is that no one can say, as a pharmacologist can say how a blood pressure drug works, what general anaesthesia is at the level of molecules.

At the turn of the twentieth century, Hans Horst Meyer and Charles Ernest Overton separately noticed that if one lines up the available anaesthetic agents and measures how readily each dissolves in olive oil, that ranking predicts almost exactly how little of each is needed to put an animal under.
The relationship held across more than four orders of magnitude of potency.
A gas that barely dissolves in oil, such as nitrous oxide, needs enormous concentrations; one that dissolves greedily works at a whisper.
The inference seemed forced: if oil solubility predicts potency, the drug must work somewhere oily, and the oiliest structure in a neuron is its lipid membrane.
The idea hardened into a unified account: anaesthetics dissolve into the bilayer, disorder it, and the ion channels there stop working.
One observation appeared to seal the case.
Animals anaesthetized and held under helium at roughly a hundred atmospheres begin to move again, as though the pressure were squeezing the membrane back to its original volume.
One site, one mechanism, no receptors required.
The account began to fail on its own terms.
Warming a membrane by a single degree disorders the bilayer more than a clinical dose of anaesthetic does, yet a mildly feverish patient does not fall asleep.
Isoflurane exists as two mirror image forms, identical in every property a bath of oil could distinguish.
In animals the two differ in potency, one being measurably more effective than the other.
Oil cannot tell left from right.
Something handed, which in a cell means a protein, must be reading the molecule.
Then came compounds that refused to cooperate: chemists built halogenated molecules whose oil solubility predicted that they ought to be powerful anaesthetics, and several of them are not.
An animal breathing one still withdraws from a surgical stimulus.
These non-immobilizers are not inactive: several impair an animal's memory for what happened while it breathed them.
A compound that erases the record of an event without abolishing the response to it is itself an argument that the old correlation was never a law.
The gentlest blow was the most damaging.
Firefly luciferase, the enzyme behind a firefly's glow, is a soluble protein with no membrane near it.
Anaesthetics switch it off, and they do so in nearly the order of their clinical potency.
If a lone protein in a test tube reproduces the century old correlation, the correlation never pointed at lipid in particular.
They are small, greasy and weakly sticky, and lodge in any oily pocket, whether in a bilayer or in the folded interior of a protein.
After that, the lipid theory lost its purchase.
The field turned to proteins and found too many of them.
Propofol, etomidate, the barbiturates and the volatile ethers all enhance the GABA type A receptor, which carries most of the brain's inhibition, so each pulse lasts longer than it should.
Glycine receptors, which do similar work in the cord, are enhanced too.
Ketamine, nitrous oxide and xenon leave GABA largely alone and instead block the NMDA glutamate receptor, cutting excitation rather than boosting inhibition.
Volatile agents also open two pore domain potassium channels, which make a neuron harder to fire, and suppress the pacemaker channels of thalamic cells.
Set the drugs side by side and the problem is visible.
Xenon is a single atom that forms almost no chemical bonds, and it is a complete anaesthetic.
Nitrous oxide is three atoms in a line.
Propofol is an oily phenol delivered as a white emulsion.
Etomidate is a small ring, alphaxalone a steroid, and the volatile agents short carbon chains hung with fluorine and chlorine.
In any other drug class the list would be absurd, since molecules that act at one receptor usually share a recognizable shape.
These share almost nothing beyond a mild reluctance to stay dissolved in water.
Depth, the operating room's word, is a metaphor.
Its most precise definition is minimum alveolar concentration, or MAC: the concentration of inhaled agent at which half of patients will not move when the skin is cut.
For isoflurane that is a little over one percent, for sevoflurane about two percent, for desflurane about six, and for xenon roughly two thirds of the breath.
For nitrous oxide it is slightly more than a whole atmosphere, so that gas cannot carry an anaesthetic alone.
MAC is both useful and blunt.
It describes a population rather than the patient on the table, and the only thing it measures is whether a body moves.
Whether a body moves is decided largely below the neck.

In animal preparations that separated the brain's blood supply from the body's, the brain alone needed far more agent to stop movement, and animals whose cords were cut off from the brain needed about the same as intact ones.
Immobility is mostly a spinal effect.
Unresponsiveness to speech, which a patient would call being under, depends on loops between thalamus and cortex and appears at perhaps a third to a half of MAC.
Amnesia appears earlier still, at something like a quarter of MAC, and leans on the hippocampus and the amygdala.
Three effects, three doses, three places.

General anaesthesia, then, is not one state but a bundle of them, assembled from several drugs: one for unconsciousness, an opioid for the reflex responses to injury, and often a muscle relaxant for stillness.
The relaxant is the awkward member: it paralyzes the patient and so removes the very sign, movement, on which the standard measure of depth was built.
This is why monitoring depth is harder than it looks.
No instrument reads experience.
The available monitors compress the electroencephalogram from a few forehead electrodes through an algorithm fitted to particular drugs and return one number from zero to one hundred.
Those numbers behave well for propofol and the ethers and badly for the rest.
Ketamine, nitrous oxide and xenon can drive the index toward apparent wakefulness in a patient who is entirely unresponsive.
Before the relaxant is given, a cuff on the upper arm keeps it from one hand, so the anaesthetist can ask the patient to squeeze.
A minority of patients squeeze on command during surgery, and almost none of them remember anything afterward.
Whether such a patient is conscious in any sense that ought to trouble us is not something a monitor can settle, and honest disagreement about it runs through the literature.
Reports of awareness with recall run about one in twenty thousand when patients must volunteer the experience, and twenty or thirty times higher when every patient is asked directly.
The distance between those two figures is itself a finding.
Why has a mechanism been so slow to arrive?
Partly because the targets are redundant.
Delete one in a mouse and the anaesthetic usually still works, shifted a little along the dose axis, as expected of a drug that binds many things weakly.
There is a celebrated exception.
Etomidate acts at a pocket in one GABA type A subunit, and changing a single amino acid there leaves mice the drug can no longer keep still.
That is as clean a result as the field has produced, and it holds for one drug, not for the state.
None of this unsettles the practice, and it should not.
Anaesthesia is a recipe refined over a century and a half by watching patients rather than deducing from theory, and the refinement has been extraordinarily successful.
The incompleteness is a research program rather than a warning.
The situation does have a particular flavor.
The field has learned to produce on demand, by the millions, a condition it cannot yet define, and the most economical description of what these drugs do is still a list of what a patient cannot do.
